## Quiz-show speed and homework patience

You already know two speeds of thinking—even if nobody gave them lab names.

Picture a quiz show. The buzzer is live. A question flashes. Your mouth answers before your mind has finished checking. Sometimes that blurt is right. Sometimes it walks straight into a trap that rewards patience.

Now picture a hard homework problem at the kitchen table. You write a first guess. You frown. You erase. You check the units. You ask whether the answer makes sense. That second pass is slower and costs effort. It is also how you catch the trap.

Neither speed is "good" or "bad" by itself. Blurts win when the room is on fire and you need the exit. Careful checks win when a wrong first answer costs a grade, a deal, or a friendship. The question in this chapter is narrower: **do drink states nudge which speed you lean on**, under timed lab tasks?

You do not need formal labels for the open story. Think **fast blurt** versus **careful check**—a dimmer of effort, not a light switch labeled genius. The pack and paper names live in the foldouts.

## Why the cup might move the dimmer

Tea patterns in these packs are described as helping keep impulsive reactions in check, with L-theanine and caffeine together linked with longer careful focus.[^2] That is not "tea makes you wise." It is closer to: *the spotlight stays steadier on a boring attention task.*

Coffee under stress can push rapid shortcuts. It may help simple arithmetic—the kind of work that rewards speed—but can suffer on complex reflective tasks when time pressure or anxiety is already high (Rogers et al., 2013; pack). Alcohol makes the fast blurt dominant and careful control drops sharply—the classic idea that intoxication narrows attention to the most immediate cues.[^3]

In everyday clothes:

- **Tea combo (as studied):** more like keeping the homework patience available a little longer.
- **High-caffeine under stress:** more like the quiz-show buzzer getting louder.
- **Alcohol:** more like the whole room shrinking to whatever is loudest right now—a joke, an insult, an unfair offer.

Same broad family of caffeine still sits in many tea designs. The pattern changes when L-theanine joins and the task rewards sustained control—not when marketing renames caffeine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: System 1 / System 2 table (formal labels)"}
Psychologists often talk about two modes (Kahneman's dual-process framing, building on earlier work with Tversky):[^1]

| Metric | System 1 (fast blurt) | System 2 (careful check) | Source frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Speed / effort | Fast, low metabolic cost | Slow, costly | Kahneman (2011) [^1] |
| Tea pattern in these packs | Helps keep impulsive reactions in check | L-theanine + caffeine synergy linked with longer careful focus | Owen et al. (2008) [^2] |
| Coffee pattern | Under stress, can push rapid shortcuts | May help simple arithmetic; can suffer on complex reflective tasks | Pack / Rogers line |
| Alcohol pattern | Becomes dominant | Careful control drops sharply | Steele & Josephs (1990) [^3] |

Dual-process work treats this as a **spectrum of effort**, not a binary drink switch. Do not read the table as "coffee = dumb, tea = wise."
:::

## A kitchen scene: blurting into a trap

Imagine a question with an intuitive wrong answer and a slower right answer—the kind of item used in reflection tests. Under a pure caffeine capsule, the packs' Brunyé-line snapshot says impulsive errors rose versus placebo.[^7] That is not "caffeine makes you stupid." It is "caffeine can speed you into the trap when the trap rewards patience."

Now flip the drink story. A theanine-plus-caffeine combination helped attention switching and cut distractibility at about an hour in Owen et al.[^2] Related vigilance snapshots in the packs show more hits and fewer false alarms.[^5] A Stroop-style interference cost (naming ink color when the word says something else) fell under L-theanine in the Higashiyama-line pack reading.[^6]

Same broad stimulant family—different pattern when L-theanine joins and the task rewards sustained control.

People love a neat slogan: "Coffee = fast thinking, tea = careful thinking." Too neat. The packs' verification note is blunt: these operations sit on a continuous spectrum of executive effort, not a binary physiological switch. Caffeine accelerates basic psychomotor speed; it degrades performance on high-complexity reflective tasks primarily under **high time-pressure** or **pre-existing anxiety**. L-theanine + caffeine stabilizes sustained attention, but its capacity to reduce cognitive biases (anchoring, framing) is heavily moderated by task structure and baseline cognitive capacity.[^1][^2]

So: caffeine can speed the blurting; under time pressure or anxiety it can hurt the careful check. L-theanine + caffeine is studied for sustained attention—**not** for deleting every bias.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: dual-process snapshots (lab doses, not slogans)"}
These are isolated lab doses—often capsules or matched drinks—not "your grocery mug at 9 a.m."

| Task | Condition | Finding | Trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Attention switching / memory distractibility | **100 mg** L-theanine + **50 mg** caffeine | Faster, more accurate switching at 60 min; less distractibility vs placebo | Owen et al. (2008) [^2] |
| Visuospatial attention + alpha EEG | Same combination | Higher hit rate and *d′*; lower tonic alpha read as engaged attention | Kelly et al. (2008) [^4] |
| RVIP vigilance | L-theanine + caffeine (Haskell line; pack) | Hits **+8.6%**; false alarms **−12.1%** | Haskell et al. (2008; pack) [^5] |
| Stroop interference | **200 mg** L-theanine (pack) | Interference cost down about **28.4 ms** | Higashiyama et al. (2011; pack) [^6] |
| Cognitive Reflection Test | **200 mg** caffeine vs placebo (pack) | Impulsive (System 1) errors up about **14.2%** | Brunyé et al. (2012; pack) [^7] |

What these tasks are *for*:

- **CRT** — traps that punish blurting the intuitive wrong answer.
- **Stroop** — naming ink color when the word says something else (inhibit automatic reading).
- **RVIP / switching** — sustained attention under load.

Alcohol makes System 1 dominant via alcohol myopia—attention narrows to the most immediate cues.[^3] Chapter 2's L-theanine story connects here: by softening excess glutamate signaling, L-theanine is linked with better sustained attention on hard switching tasks (see [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd) and [2.1 Brain action](../module-02/01-brain-action.qmd)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: how to read a 'tea makes you wiser' headline"}
Ask four questions before you believe the headline:

1. **Which task?** CRT, Stroop, RVIP, and "real negotiation" are not interchangeable.
2. **Which dose?** **100/50**, **200** L-theanine, **200** caffeine—or a cafe latte of unknown mg?
3. **Which timing?** Many attention designs land near **+40 to +60 minutes**—see [4.4](04-study-protocols.qmd).
4. **Which contrast?** Placebo capsule, decaf, water, or "no drink"? Expectation matters.

If those answers are missing, keep the finding on the "interesting hint" shelf—not the "life rule" shelf.
:::

## Alcohol as the extreme contrast

If tea-combo studies are about *sustaining* careful attention, alcohol studies are about *narrowing* it. Steele and Josephs's alcohol-myopia idea: intoxication shrinks the spotlight to whatever is most immediate—sometimes a joke, sometimes an insult, sometimes an unfair offer.[^3]

That extreme contrast helps beginners. You do not need to believe "tea = careful thinking" to believe "drinks can move the spotlight." Alcohol yanks the spotlight inward and short-range. L-theanine + caffeine designs more often try to keep the spotlight steady on a boring vigilance task. Different directions on the same dimmer metaphor.

## What "careful focus" is not

L-theanine + caffeine helping vigilance hits is not the same as:

- removing framing effects in a pricing decision,
- fixing anchoring on a random number, or
- making you wise in a negotiation with incomplete information.

The packs say bias reduction is task- and person-dependent. Hold that fence whenever a headline upgrades "better vigilance" into "better judgment about everything."

## Bridge to Module 2 (and why false alarms matter)

Chapter 2's L-theanine story was about quieter excitatory noise and calmer stress markers. Chapter 4's attention batteries ask whether that quieter control shows up as fewer false alarms and better switching. The linkage page stitches those claims; this lesson keeps the doses honest ([2.1 Brain action](../module-02/01-brain-action.qmd); [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd)).

Speed of thinking is one axis. Appetite for risk—and patience for tomorrow—is another. That is the next sitting.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: spectrum language for beginners"}
Think of executive effort like a dimmer, not a light switch.

- Low effort / fast: habits, first guesses, emotional reactions.
- High effort / slow: checking, inhibiting, recomputing.

Drinks nudge where the dimmer sits under load. They do not install a new personality. Anxiety and time pressure matter as much as milligrams—the packs say so explicitly in the heuristic-switch verification note.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: take-home checklist for Lesson 4.1"}
1. Open story = fast blurt vs careful check; formal System 1/2 labels live in foldouts.[^1]
2. Tea combo → sustained attention pattern in cited designs—not "wiser about everything."[^2]
3. Pure caffeine can speed you into reflection traps under pressure.[^7]
4. Alcohol myopia = spotlight shrinks to the immediate.[^3]
5. Ask task / dose / timing / contrast before believing a headline.
6. Next: losses that sting and tomorrows that fade—still no invented tea-and-markets theory.
:::

## Story in one minute

Quiz-show speed blurts; homework patience checks. Tea-plus-caffeine designs in the packs more often help sustained attention than they install a new personality. Pure caffeine can speed you into reflection traps under pressure; alcohol shrinks the spotlight to the immediate. Formal System 1/2 labels and dose tables live behind the click.

::: {.callout-tip title="You can stop here"}
- Everyday idea: quiz-show blurt vs homework patience—formal System 1/2 labels live in foldouts.
- Tea combo → sustained attention in cited designs—not "wiser about everything."
- Ask task / dose / timing / contrast before believing a headline.
:::
